rows.title: The backend platform — Rules
rows.summary: 1. The platform names no dialect.
body: 1. **The platform names no dialect.** `docs/07-reference/backend.md`, the brief, `platform.toml` and the `.nuc` of
the examples hold only Nuclear and Nuclear's own library; a name of a target's library there is a bug. How a
dialect writes a kind is in that dialect's reference, never here.
2. **Kinds and features never differ between the dialects.** A feature is written once in Nuclear and every dialect
implements it: the platform's reference gets the Nuclear, each dialect's reference its output, both checks run
it. `tasks_api` must keep building with every dialect.
3. **`platform.toml` is the contract.** A kind, a decorator or a plugin a dialect uses is listed there, or the
loader refuses the dialect (N0305). The rules of a decorator are data there (`[decorators.args]`,
`[decorators.fields]`): no decorator name is written in Rust.
4. **The runtimes behave the same.** A behaviour added to one is added to the other, with the same test in both
(`packages/synapsis-py/tests/test_data.py`, `packages/synapsis-nest/test/data.test.ts`; the types of a body
and a model built in code: `tests/test_types.py`, `test/types.test.ts`; the guards and the WebSocket:
`tests/test_sockets.py`, `test/sockets.test.ts`). The database check compares their answers on every
database: a change of the data words runs it.

rows.title: The backend platform — Rules
rows.summary: 5. A changed public API of a runtime means its type definitions are regenerated (runbook).
body: 5. **A changed public API of a runtime** means its type definitions are regenerated
([runbook](docs/06-runbooks/change-a-runtime.md)).
6. **The examples are goldens.** Output that changed on purpose: `UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 cargo test`, then review the diff.
7. **A file's name in `docs/07-reference/` and `docs/08-guides/` is its topic**: `nuclear help backend` and
`nuclear spec --brief` find them by name, and the installer copies both folders with `platform.toml` and
`packages/`. They are normative: changed only with the feature they describe.
8. Done = `cargo test`, `cargo clippy --all-targets` and both checks green, the reference and these documents
updated in the same change, `docs/01-product/roadmap.md` current.

rows.title: The backend platform
rows.summary: The backend platform of Synapsis: HTTP APIs, databases with relations, migrations and transactions, events, AI agents and graphs, written once in Nuclear and built with any of its dialects.
body: The backend platform of Synapsis: HTTP APIs, databases with relations, migrations and transactions, events, AI
agents and graphs, written once in Nuclear and built with any of its dialects. This folder holds what is the same
for every dialect: the contract (`platform.toml`), the runtime packages the generated code runs on, the examples
and the checks. The Nuclear of a backend project never changes when its dialect changes.
Paths in these documents are relative to this folder (`nuclear-synapsis-framework/platforms/backend/`); a path that
starts with `nuclearlang/`, `nuclear-synapsis-framework/`, `tools/`, `installer/` or `.github/` starts at the root
of the tree. The rules of the whole platform are in [the root `AGENTS.md`](../../../AGENTS.md).

body: The database check now fails on any difference between the schemas the two dialects leave (none on SQLite,
PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB) and runs 12 migration scenarios with the real command.
- **Migrations that hold on every database** (`nuclear migrate`, reference §2.8), the same in `fastapi` and `nestjs`:
the same lines printed, the same exit codes, the same rules. New: `nuclear migrate status` (every migration:
applied or pending), `nuclear migrate --to <migration>` and `nuclear migrate down --to <migration>`. The rules:
- the history is one line: two migrations made after the same one, or one the database has and the folder does
not, are refused by every command;
- each migration runs in a transaction of its own: a failed one stays pending, and PostgreSQL and SQLite keep
nothing of it (MySQL and MariaDB cannot undo a schema change: the message says what is left);
- every unique and foreign key has a name (`uq_<table>_<column>`, `fk_<table>_<column>`), so it can be dropped;
- `make` also warns of a required column added without a default and of a column that becomes required; two
migrations made in the same second get different names;
- migrations made before this version still run.

rows.title: Vision — Constraints
rows.summary: readable Nuclear.
body: - The golden rule of the whole platform: generated code as fast as an expert's, instant transpilation, minimal
readable Nuclear.
- The user's rule for the data words: the code looks as much alike as possible across the platforms, at the middle
point of cost and benefit (the key decorator and `paginate` are the same word on backend and mobile).
- A feature is delivered in every dialect at once: the reference gets the Nuclear, each dialect's reference its
output, and both checks run it.

rows.title: Vision — The problem
rows.summary: A backend written in Nuclear holds only its business logic: the kinds write the framework code, the dependencies, the JSON, the validation and the routes.
body: A backend written in Nuclear holds only its business logic: the kinds write the framework code, the dependencies,
the JSON, the validation and the routes. The backend platform is the list of what such a project may write (its
kinds, decorators, folders, `config.nuc`, plugins and tests) and it is the same for every dialect, so one project
builds as the project of more than one technology and its Nuclear never changes when its dialect changes.
It covers HTTP APIs, data (entities with relations, repositories, pagination, transactions, migrations), events
and a cache, and AI (tools, agents, states, graphs).

rows.title: Vision — What it does not do
rows.summary: project.
body: - It does not say how a dialect writes its target. That is each dialect's reference, in its language's dialect
project.
- It has no kind, decorator or feature that exists in one dialect only. The one thing that ties code to a dialect is
using that dialect's type definitions (a library that exists only in its language).
- It never loads a relation by itself: no lazy query, no eager loading by default
([ADR-backend-0001](../03-adr/0001-backend-data.md)).
- It is not the `nuclear` command: what `new`, `build`, `run`, `test` and `migrate` do is the dialect's
`[toolchain]`, run by [the command line tools](../../../../../tools/cli/AGENTS.md).
- Not there yet ([roadmap](../01-product/roadmap.md)): authentication, guards and sessions; background jobs; file
uploads; a Dockerfile; observability.

rows.title: Vision — Who uses it
rows.summary: (`nuclear help backend`) and the brief, and never a dialect's documents to know what to write.
body: - **A person or an AI agent writing a backend**: they read [the reference](../07-reference/backend.md)
(`nuclear help backend`) and [the brief](../07-reference/brief/backend.md), and never a dialect's documents to
know what to write.
- **An app of the mobile or web platform**: it gets its models and repositories generated from a backend's contract
([the guide](../08-guides/contracts.md)).
- **The author of a dialect**: `platform.toml` says what the dialect must implement; the rules of the data
decorators come with it, so a new backend dialect gets them by writing templates.
- **Whoever changes a runtime** (`packages/`): the code every generated backend runs on.

rows.summary: relation that was not asked for is never queried.
body: - **Relations**: `many_to_one`, `one_to_many`, `many_to_many`, `one_to_one` in `orm.py`, all `lazy="raise"`: a
relation that was not asked for is never queried. The foreign key is appended to the table in
`Entity.__init_subclass__`. Join tables are made when the mappers are configured, so `Database.open` calls
`configure_mappers()`; SQLite runs `PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON`.
- **Answers**: `wire_of` turns a row and every related row that was loaded into their schemas (`schema_of`), so
the JSON has Nuclear's names at every level; `EntitySchema` leaves an unloaded relation out. A `DateTime` is
written as `toIso()` writes it (`models.wire_date`: UTC, milliseconds, `Z`), in entities and models.
- **A route's parameters** keep Nuclear's names for the client: `{customerId}` and `?minTotal=` reach
`customer_id` and `min_total` (`web._public`).
- **Columns**: a `DateTime` is `UtcDateTime` (written in UTC and read back in UTC on every database: SQLite, MySQL
and MariaDB keep no time zone; its `load_dialect_impl` names the column with its fraction: `DATETIME(6)` on
MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite, `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` on PostgreSQL); a text without `length` is `String(255)`, as the other runtime; the mapper reads
back what the database writes (`eager_defaults`: `@created`, `@updated`, defaults), so the row a use case answers

- **Defaults**: a field's default is also the column's SQL default (`column(default=...)` sets `server_default`),

rows.summary: order of `id`.
body: - The history is the table `migrations` (`_history_table`: `id`, `timestamp`, `name`), read by `_history` in the
order of `id`. When it is missing it is made, from `alembic_version` if the database was migrated before 0.93

run (`all`), one per migration (`each`) or an engine in `AUTOCOMMIT` (`none`). SQLite's driver is opened with
`autocommit=False`, or a schema change would run outside the transaction; after each migration
`PRAGMA foreign_key_check` must be empty.

a table of SQLite from what it reads in the database; `_reflected` (a `column_reflect` listener) says the three
things that are not read there: `AUTOINCREMENT`, the name of a constraint made without one, and the fraction of a
`DateTime` (`DATETIME(6)` is read as `DATETIME`).

body: What the database refuses for integrity answers 409 `conflict` (the platform's reference §2.4; Spring Data REST's
answer to Spring's `DataIntegrityViolationException`): `create_app` handles SQLAlchemy's `IntegrityError` (a unique,
a foreign key, a required column, on the four databases) and `errors.IntegrityViolation`, which `repository._fits`
raises from `save` and `update` for a text longer than its column (counted with `len`: code points). The exception
leaves `@transactional` through its `session.begin()`, which rolls back. Test:
`test_what_the_database_refuses_for_integrity_is_a_409` (the same cases as `data.test.ts`).
An exact column is `ExactInteger()` / `ExactDecimal(p, s)` in a migration (`_render`; the file imports them). SQLite
keeps their words (`EXACT TEXT(p,s)`): `_reflected` reads them back as the exact types and `_compare_type` compares
them, so `make` sees a changed precision or scale; after each migration applied on SQLite, `_exact_texts` writes the
texts of every `EXACT TEXT(p,s)` column again with its decimals (rounded half away from zero, as the other databases
convert the column; a value with more digits than the column takes fails the migration). Test:
`test_an_exact_column_is_made_and_changed_by_its_precision_and_scale`.

rows.title: The Python runtime: `synapsis-py` — Migrations
rows.summary: migration is `versions/<timestamp>_<slug>.py` with `upgrade()` and `downgrade()` over `op`, loaded as a module and run inside `Operations.context` (`_apply`).
body: - Alembic writes and runs the operations; its revisions, its `env.py` and its `alembic_version` are not used. A
migration is `versions/<timestamp>_<slug>.py` with `upgrade()` and `downgrade()` over `op`, loaded as a module
and run inside `Operations.context` (`_apply`). The files are ordered by their name (`_files`).
- `make` never reads the database: it runs every migration on an empty SQLite in memory and asks Alembic's
autogenerate for the difference with the entities (`produce_migrations`, `render_python_code`, in batch mode).
`_prepare` names every unique and foreign key the migration makes or drops (`uq_<table>_<column>`,
`fk_<table>_<column>`) and collects the warnings. A changed key is compared here, because Alembic does not see
it, and refused. The entities carry no constraint names, so a migration of before 0.91 still compares equal.
- `make --rename` (`_renamed`): each rename is checked against the SQLite the migrations made and the entities, made
there (`ALTER TABLE ... RENAME`), and written as a line of the file before what autogenerate finds: Alembic's
`op.rename_table`, and `rename_column` (this module's: one `ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN` on every database,
where Alembic's `alter_column` rebuilds the table on SQLite and needs the whole column on MySQL). The way back is
the same lines reversed, last.

rows.summary: A text column is `String(n)` (`orm.TEXT_LENGTH` = 255 without `length`).
body: A text column is `String(n)` (`orm.TEXT_LENGTH` = 255 without `length`). `orm.text_type(dialect, n)` is the one
rule of its type (the same as `textType` of synapsis-nest), and `orm._text` compiles every `String(n)` with it on
PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB: an entity, `createTables` and a migration (`sa.String(length=n)`) all name the same
type.
`synapsis.migrate` is what `nuclear migrate` runs (the dialect's `[toolchain]` keys `migrate_make`, `migrate`,
`migrate_down`, `migrate_status`):
```sh
python -m synapsis.migrate make "add done to tasks" --dir <migrations>   # one migration: the entities minus the migrations
python -m synapsis.migrate up [--to <name>] --dir <migrations>           # applies the pending ones
python -m synapsis.migrate down [--to <name>] --dir <migrations>         # reverts the last one applied, or every one applied after <name>
python -m synapsis.migrate status --dir <migrations>                     # every migration: applied or pending
# up, down: --fake (only the history changes), --transaction all|each|none (default all)

column's decimals); the repository finds an exact column by its type (`BIGINT`, `DECIMAL`), writes a value as a

by value (`liteCompare`, `liteOrder`: the same SQL as the other runtime); `fits` refuses what the column cannot
hold. `IsBigInt` / `IsBigDouble` / `MinExact` / `MaxExact` are the model's; `BigIntPipe` / `BigDoublePipe` the
parameters'; the app's `json replacer` writes a `bigint`, `Entity.toJSON` keeps the columns in their order.

opens on the database of the last repository made ([roadmap](../01-product/roadmap.md)).

writes in the other runtime.

optional field of a model left `undefined` (the fields class-validator's `IsOptional` marks, read once per class),

- **`@created` / `@updated`** are Sequelize's `@CreatedAt` / `@UpdatedAt`: the app's clock (`new Date()`, to the

`Date` of a number) and takes a text only; `reasonsOf` names the item of a list that breaks its type
(`tags.1`), which class-validator does not.
- **A model built in code** is checked by its constructor when it is given values (`checkModel`:
`validateSync`, `InvalidModel` with the same reasons as a body). class-transformer builds the body of a request
without values, so the pipe checks it once.
- **Columns**: a `DateTime` is `DataType.DATE(6)`; Sequelize writes the milliseconds only to a column with a
length.
- **Types**: `Related<T>` types a single relation, so the decorator metadata never reads the other class (two ES
modules that import each other).

body: - The entry points are apart so a production install without `@nestjs/testing`, the AI libraries or a broker's
client still loads the base (they are optional peers: [dependencies](dependencies.md)).
- `ChromaStore` is chromadb's client behind a LangChain `VectorStore`. `@langchain/community` was rejected: its

reference §2.7).
- Nest's body parsers are off (`bodyParser: false` in `createApp` and `startTestApp`): the edge reads the body, the
global `BodyPipe` parses it only for a route that takes one, and class-validator runs on the body only

(`refusedTogether`, with its metadata) so it refuses the parameters together, before the body.

router itself before Nest adds the routes. The logger has colours only in a terminal (`NO_COLOR` too).
- In the tests the databases are SQLite in memory (`SYNAPSIS_DATABASE=memory`, set by `startTestApp`).
